A Capture, a Killing, and a Congress Struggling to Keep Up

This week: an extraordinary military operation in Venezuela tested war powers, a fatal ICE shooting in Minneapolis convulsed a city, and the Justice Department's transparency failures deepened.

```markdown This was a week in which two extraordinary stories ran on parallel tracks — one involving the capture of a foreign head of state, the other the killing of an American citizen by a federal agent — while a quieter, slower story about government transparency kept grinding forward beneath them. By the time the week closed, Congress had begun, unevenly, to reassert itself against an executive branch that had spent six days acting largely on its own terms.

The weekend opened with the aftershock of an operation few in Washington had seen coming. President Trump had ordered a military mission that captured Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro, and had done so without notifying the congressional "Gang of Eight," the small group of leaders normally briefed on sensitive military and intelligence operations regardless of party. The bypassing of that norm set off protests in major American cities, with demonstrators demanding that Congress assert oversight, even as the House failed to take any immediate action despite scattered calls for impeachment. Elsewhere, the weekend carried its own smaller signals of change and strain. In New York, Zohran Mamdani was sworn in as mayor and moved immediately to revoke the executive orders of his predecessor, Eric Adams, following Adams's federal corruption indictment — a symbolic first act aimed at accountability. Across federal agencies, meanwhile, came early signs of a different kind of erosion: cuts to climate-resilience funding, reduced staffing at NOAA and the National Weather Service, the disbanding of science advisory councils, and new spending restrictions imposed on FEMA, all chipping away at the government's capacity to prepare for disasters. Separately, the Justice Department's senior ethics attorney was fired without explanation, and in Texas, a detainee's death in ICE custody was expected to be ruled a homicide.

By Monday, the legal machinery around Maduro was already in motion. He was arraigned in a Manhattan federal courtroom and pleaded not guilty to narco-terrorism and related charges — an appearance without real precedent, a sitting foreign head of state, captured by the U.S. military, now facing an American jury. The same day, two members of the Gang of Eight, Representative Jim Himes and Senator Chuck Schumer, said publicly that they had never been briefed on the Venezuela operation at all; Himes went further, accusing officials of having misled Congress earlier about military plans in the region. Monday also brought the Justice Department's lawsuit against 22 states, most led by Democratic secretaries of state, over their refusal to hand over complete voter rolls containing sensitive personal data — part of a stated effort to build a national voter file. In Arizona, the state Supreme Court building was evacuated after vials testing positive for a homemade explosive were found inside, an unsettling reminder of the vulnerability of judicial institutions. And in a development that would gain significance later in the week, Paul Singer's Elliott Investment Management acquired Citgo, Venezuela's U.S. oil subsidiary, for $5.9 billion — a price well below the company's estimated value — with reporting suggesting the military operation had opened a door for a politically aligned billionaire to walk through.

Tuesday shifted attention toward a different kind of institutional failure. Court filings revealed that the Department of Justice had released barely over 12,000 documents under the Epstein Files Transparency Act — less than one percent of what the law required — having already missed its December 19 deadline. Democrats pressed for an unredacted accounting of implicated officials, but none arrived. Maduro's legal case advanced further, as he was formally charged with drug-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine-importation conspiracy, and weapons possession, facing a possible life sentence. In the House, the death of Representative Doug LaMalfa narrowed the Republican majority to a razor-thin 218–213, tightening the margins for any future legislative fight. The administration also sued two California cities, Morgan Hill and Petaluma, over local ordinances restricting natural gas infrastructure, arguing federal preemption — part of a broader campaign against local climate policy. And in Minnesota, the day's most consequential development took shape almost quietly: ICE and Homeland Security Investigations agents began surging into the state under "Operation Metro Surge," the largest such operation to date, drawing early community protest that would explode into something much larger within twenty-four hours.

That explosion came Wednesday. During the immigration surge in Minneapolis, an ICE agent shot and killed Renee Nicole Good, a 37-year-old U.S. citizen and mother, as she drove away from federal agents. The Department of Homeland Security described the shooting as self-defense, but video evidence reviewed by Reuters showed her vehicle moving away from officers at the time she was shot — a direct contradiction of the official account. Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey and Governor Tim Walz condemned the killing immediately. In the same enforcement wave, a second federal officer shot a man in the leg during a separate arrest attempt, compounding the tension already gripping the city. Wednesday also brought a striking act of historical revision: the White House issued a statement describing the January 6 Capitol attackers as "peaceful patriotic protesters," contradicting the documented injuries of more than 140 police officers that day. In Virginia, a federal judge ordered Trump-appointed lawyer Lindsey Halligan to explain why she continued using the title "U.S. Attorney" after a prior ruling had found her appointment unlawful — she had kept signing indictments in the meantime. And separately, 29 Senate Democrats demanded an accounting of law enforcement personnel redirected to ICE, arguing the reassignments were pulling resources from trafficking and cartel investigations.

By Thursday, both of the week's anchor stories reached turning points. The Senate passed a War Powers Resolution, 52–47, with five Republicans joining Democrats to require congressional authorization for any further military action in Venezuela. Trump responded by threatening a veto and asserting unilateral authority to act throughout the Western Hemisphere, criticizing the Republicans who had broken ranks. At the same time, the FBI assumed exclusive control of the investigation into Renee Good's death, cutting off the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension from evidence and case materials. Governor Walz and local officials called the move an attempt to control the outcome; Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem framed it as a simple matter of jurisdiction. Vice President JD Vance then went further, publicly defending the ICE officer involved, criticizing media coverage of the shooting, and alleging without evidence that Good had been part of a "leftwing network" — even as DHS labeled the incident domestic terrorism despite eyewitness video suggesting otherwise. Elsewhere, the House passed a bipartisan bill extending Affordable Care Act tax credits for three years, 230–196, with 17 Republicans joining Democrats. A federal judge disqualified a second unlawfully appointed U.S. attorney, John Sarcone, from investigating New York Attorney General Letitia James — the fifth such Trump-installed prosecutor removed by a court. Draft plans surfaced showing the administration considering cutting FEMA's workforce by more than half. Representatives Ro Khanna and Thomas Massie asked a federal judge to appoint a special master to force DOJ compliance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act. And Trump announced Venezuela would ship 30 to 50 million barrels of oil to the United States, relaxing the embargo just days after the military operation — a shift that stood to benefit Gulf Coast refineries, including the newly discounted Citgo.

Friday drew several of these threads to a head. Attorney General Pam Bondi formally admitted in a letter to a federal judge that the Justice Department had failed to disclose more than 99 percent of Epstein-related files, confirming what the week's court filings had already suggested — that the department's earlier claims of progress had not matched reality. Trump signed an executive order declaring a national emergency to shield Venezuelan oil revenue held in U.S. accounts from judicial process, placing control over the disbursement of those funds squarely with the executive branch. Representative Robin Kelly filed three articles of impeachment against Secretary Noem over the handling of the Good shooting, accusing her of obstruction of justice, violation of public trust, and self-dealing. A federal court in the Southern District of New York blocked the Administration for Children and Families from freezing Child Care Development Fund, TANF, and Social Services Block Grant disbursements to states. And across the country, protests over Good's death continued to spread — organizers including Indivisible and the 50501 Movement planned more than a thousand demonstrations under the banner of a "Free America Walkout," and one protester was permanently blinded by non-lethal ammunition during the unrest. The week's final data points arrived almost as an afterthought: a weak December jobs report showing only 50,000 jobs added, the worst year for job growth outside a recession since 2003; Ford's announced shift away from electric vehicle production following the cancellation of EV subsidies; and an accusation that Trump himself had leaked confidential jobs data ahead of its official release.

Taken as a whole, the week showed several branches of government straining against each other in real time. A military operation abroad proceeded without the congressional notification that war-powers law presumes, and it took the Senate the better part of a week to respond with anything more than words. A fatal shooting on American soil produced two irreconcilable accounts of the same video footage, with the federal government moving to control both the investigation and the narrative before independent scrutiny could take hold. A transparency law passed with bipartisan intent continued to be ignored by the agency charged with enforcing it, moving from missed deadlines to open admission without any accompanying compliance. And even as courts intervened repeatedly — disqualifying unlawfully appointed prosecutors, blocking a funding freeze, questioning executive claims to unilateral authority — the pace of executive action continued to outrun the capacity of Congress, and in several instances the public record itself, to keep up. ```
